podcast.title: First Version Disbandment (2001-2002)
podcast.body: The first iteration of Big Wreck concluded around 2001 or 2002, with Ian Thorneley subsequently pursuing other musical projects. "But that first version of the band was done by 2002."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Albatross Album Naming
podcast.body: The album "Albatross" was named after its titular song, which itself was named when the word "Albatross" simply "fell into" Ian Thorneley's lap during writing, rather than a conscious reference to the Rime of the Ancient Mariner or John Cleese's sketch. The general practice for naming albums is to choose a song title, with "In Loving Memory" and "But for the Sun" being exceptions. "Dude, I just named the album after the song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Contrast between Industry 1.0 and 2.0
podcast.body: Ian Thorneley noted a significant difference in the music industry between Big Wreck's first and second versions. The initial era involved experiences like being wined and dined by label executives such as Ahmet Ertegun, while the later period with SRO Anthem offered more creative freedom without the commercial pressures of chasing hits. "The music industry of Big Rec version 1.0. It was very different from what you had to deal with Big Rec version 2.0."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Creative Conflict with Atlantic Records
podcast.body: For their second album, Atlantic Records pressured Big Wreck to adopt a sound similar to Nickelback, aiming for a more "packaged" and commercially viable product. The band, however, desired to move in a more experimental direction, creating significant tension and contributing to the eventual dissolution of the original lineup. "They needed to nickel back. They wanted, that's totally what they wanted."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Formation in Boston
podcast.body: Big Wreck was formed in Boston, Massachusetts, out of collaborations between Ian Thornley, Brian Doherty, Dave Henning, and Forest Williams, who had met while attending Berklee School of Music. "It was formed in Boston."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Management Trust Affiliation
podcast.body: Big Wreck was managed by The Management Trust, a Canadian management company known for also representing The Tragically Hip, The Watchmen, and Andrew Cash at the time. The Management Trust played a crucial role in securing studio time and facilitating the band's early career development. "We had, we had management. We had the management trust."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Recording at The Bath House
podcast.body: Big Wreck recorded at The Bath House, The Tragically Hip's residential studio. "Blue rodeo, Ronnie Hawkins, Sam Roberts, Big Rec, and dozens and dozens of others have worked there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: More Famous Recording Studios

podcast.title: Reformation as Big Wreck Version 2.0
podcast.body: The band reunited around 2010-2011, initiated by Ian Thorneley missing the connection with former members. A Thorneley tour stop near Sarnia, where Brian Dorody lived, led to Dorody filling in for a show when the existing guitarist was unavailable, sparking the idea for a new Big Wreck era. "And then all of a sudden, there's Big Rec version 2."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Ruben Huzenga's Collaboration
podcast.body: Guitarist Ruben Huzenga, formerly of Glüleg, collaborated with Big Wreck in his personal studio. This illustrates his continued involvement in Canadian music production and inter-band relationships. "Ruben Huzenga has his own studio where he's worked with Edwin and also with Big Rec."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Search for a Singer
podcast.body: Initially, Big Wreck struggled to find a suitable singer, leading to Ian Thornley reluctantly taking on the vocal duties himself. They even tried out one singer who turned out to be associated with a "gang" and was suspected of stealing from the band's van, leading to his swift dismissal. "How did you end up singing? Because we couldn't find one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Version 1.0 Dissolution
podcast.body: The original lineup of Big Wreck (version 1.0) lasted for exactly two albums, with its breakup influenced by factors including record label interference, extremely long touring periods (up to 18 months straight), and internal conflicts within the band. "So big rec version 1.0 lasts exactly two albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Anecdotes with Ahmet Ertegun
xref.body: During Big Wreck's first iteration, Ian Thorneley had experiences with Ahmet Ertegun, co-founder of Atlantic Records, including a dinner at his office where Ertegun heard Big Wreck's music and shared stories about bands like the Rolling Stones and Led Zeppelin. Ertegun was described as a small Turkish man with a perfectly manicured mustache, often accompanied by "Amazonian gorgeous women." "Did you actually go for dinner with Ahmed Erdogan? Yeah, I mean, I was brought up to his office by Craig Calman."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Childhood Friend of Brian Doherty
xref.body: Dave Henning grew up with Brian Doherty in New York and roomed with him at Berklee School of Music, next door to Ian Thornley. He was an "obvious choice" for the bassist position in Big Wreck due to his existing connection with Brian. "Dave Hending was the obvious choice because he was, you know, grew up with Brian."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Creative Differences with Management
xref.body: Brian Dorody, a holdover from Big Wreck, was initially excluded from the Thorneley lineup because management felt his presence would make the new band too similar to Big Wreck, aiming for Thorneley to be a "separate sort of thing." This decision added strain to relationships. "Brian was initially going to be the other guitar player in Thorneley. And then the sort of what's called the grown-ups, the people on the other side of the desk, where like, it's too much like Big Rec of Brian's around."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Engineer for Big Wreck Demos
xref.body: Matti Mateo was the engineer at Presence studio who worked with Big Wreck on their early demos. Ian Thornley and the band "really got on with him" during the recording sessions. "particularly the engineer who was Matti Mateo and really got on with him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Formation of the Band
xref.body: After the first Big Wreck disbanded, Ian Thorneley moved to Toronto, got married, and began writing, leading to the formation of the band "Thorneley." The lineup, except for Brian Dorody, was new. "His relationship with Chad Kruger of Nickelback led him deciding with 604 Records out of Vancouver. And this was the beginning of a brand new band simply called Thorneley..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Ian Thorneley's Session Work
xref.body: Ian Thorneley worked as a session player for Nickelback, among other artists, after the initial breakup of Big Wreck. "If you look in the line of notes for albums by Nickelback and Sarah Harmer and Stephen Fearing, you'll see his name."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Jeff Burles' Role as Drummer
xref.body: Jeff Burles, drummer for The Tea Party, played drums for several Thorneley shows, including a significant gig in Edmonton, before the full reformation of Big Wreck. "Jeff Burles from the Tea Party was actually a drummer at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Left Big Wreck Temporarily
xref.body: During a summer spent in Portland, Maine, Brian Doherty temporarily left Big Wreck, stating, "I can't do this anymore. I'm going back to New York." He returned to New York to work in construction and carpentry. "Brian had said, I'm out. I can't do this anymore. I'm going back to New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Management Trust Client
xref.body: The Tragically Hip were managed by The Management Trust, the same company that managed Big Wreck and The Watchmen. "the tragically hipst management."

xref.title: Management Trust Client
xref.body: The Watchmen were managed by The Management Trust, the same company that managed The Tragically Hip and Big Wreck. "And the watchman at that time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Management Trust Member
xref.body: Alan Gregg was part of The Management Trust, Big Wreck's management company. He was instrumental in helping Ian Thornley regain entry to the US after his student visa expired, facilitating the reunion of the band. "It was Alan Greg and Alan was like, well, yeah, you know, he knows people. So he called people, got me back down there and put the band through the ringer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Met Ian Thornley at Berklee
xref.body: Forest Williams, the bassist for Big Wreck, met Ian Thornley on the third floor of their dorms at Berklee School of Music. "I had already met Forest, and I was on the third floor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Opening Act
xref.body: Big Wreck opened a few shows for The Watchmen during a summer in Canada. "we opened a few shows for the headstone and a few shows for the watchman."

xref.title: Post-Big Wreck Version 1.0 Career Transition
xref.body: After Big Wreck's initial disbandment around 2001-2002, Ian Thorneley moved back to Toronto and found work as a session player. He contributed to albums by artists such as Nickelback, Sarah Harmer, and Stephen Fearing. "After big rec version 1.0 broke up, Ian moved back to Toronto where he found work as a session player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Producer of Big Wreck Demos
xref.body: Chris Wardman produced Big Wreck's initial demo recordings at Presence studio, funded by The Management Trust. "the management trusted put up money for us to go in the studio with Chris Wardman."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Ruben Huzenga's Post-Band Career
xref.body: Guitarist Ruben Huzenga now owns and operates his own studio, where he has collaborated with Edwin and Big Wreck. This indicates his continued engagement in music production and collaboration within the Canadian scene. "Guitarist Ruben Huzenga has his own studio where he's worked with Edwin and also with Big Rec."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

xref.title: Touring and Lineup Changes
xref.body: The band Thorneley engaged in tours, including one where guitarist Paula announced she would be absent for a gig in Edmonton due to her honeymoon. This unexpected vacancy led to Brian Dorody filling in, which subsequently contributed to the reformation of Big Wreck. "Paula was like, oh, by the way, that gig in Edmonton, I'm not going to be there. As I'm going on my honeymoon in Portugal..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
